title: Energy Systems
tagline: Energy resources, steam and gas-turbine power plants, combined cycles, engines, refrigeration and air conditioning, solar, wind and hydro power, storage, cost and emissions
summary: Energy systems convert fuels, heat, wind and sunlight into the electricity, heating and cooling that society uses. The course applies thermodynamics and heat transfer to steam and gas-turbine power plants, combined cycles and cogeneration, internal combustion engines, refrigeration, heat pumps and air conditioning, solar, wind and hydropower and energy storage, and compares systems by efficiency, cost and emissions.
overview: Energy systems engineering asks how fuels, heat, wind, falling water and sunlight are turned into the electricity, motive power, heating and cooling that society uses — and at what efficiency, cost and emission. The tools are the ones you already have: the first and second laws of thermodynamics, the control-volume balances of fluid mechanics and the rate equations of heat transfer. What is new is the scale and the bookkeeping. A power station converts gigawatts, so a one-percentage-point gain in efficiency is worth millions a year; and every comparison between technologies must be made on a common basis of primary energy, capacity factor, levelised cost and life-cycle emissions.

The course opens with the energy overview: units, primary and final energy, conversion chains and the Sankey diagram, and why a kilowatt-hour of electricity from a thermal plant costs two to three kilowatt-hours of fuel. It then works through the thermal conversion technologies — practical steam plants (fossil, biomass and nuclear), gas turbines with heat-recovery steam generators, combined cycles and cogeneration, spark- and compression-ignition engines — and the reversed cycles of refrigeration, heat pumps and air conditioning. Each is analysed from the cycle and component level to plant performance (heat rate, specific fuel consumption, coefficient of performance).

The renewable chapters treat solar radiation, collectors and photovoltaic cells; wind turbines (actuator-disc theory, the Betz limit, wind statistics and capacity factor) and hydropower; and the storage technologies — pumped hydro, compressed air, flywheels, thermal stores, batteries and hydrogen — that match variable supply to demand. The last chapter brings everything to a common yardstick: discounting, the levelised cost of energy, emission factors, carbon pricing and life-cycle assessment.

Two habits make the subject manageable. First, always ask which energy you mean — fuel heating value (LHV or HHV), heat, shaft work or electricity — and which efficiency links them. Second, separate what is fixed by physics (Carnot, Betz, Shockley–Queisser limits) from what changes with technology and markets (turbine inlet temperatures, module prices, battery costs): the first you derive, the second you quote with a date and a source.
outcomes: Convert between energy and power units and trace an energy conversion chain from primary energy to useful service, computing the overall efficiency and the losses at each step.
Analyse practical Rankine steam plants with reheat and feedwater heating, and calculate cycle efficiency, plant heat rate, steam and cooling-water flows.
Calculate the performance of real gas turbines and of combined-cycle and cogeneration plants, including HRSG pinch-point analysis and fuel utilisation.
Relate the geometry, mean effective pressure, volumetric and thermal efficiency of an internal combustion engine to its power output and specific fuel consumption.
Analyse vapour-compression refrigerators and heat pumps and the psychrometric processes of air conditioning with mass and energy balances.
Estimate solar irradiation on a tilted surface and predict the output of solar thermal collectors and photovoltaic arrays.
Derive the Betz limit, estimate wind-turbine energy yield from wind statistics, and size a hydroelectric plant from head and flow.
Compare energy storage technologies by capacity, power, duration, round-trip efficiency and cost, and size a store for a given duty.
Calculate the levelised cost of energy and the emission intensity of a generating technology, and interpret the results of a life-cycle assessment.

history.title: Newcomen's atmospheric engine
history.detail: Thomas Newcomen's engine near Dudley Castle pumped water from a mine by condensing steam under a piston and letting the atmosphere push it down — the first practical machine to turn heat into work, at well under 1 % efficiency.

history.title: Watt's separate condenser
history.detail: James Watt's patent moved condensation out of the working cylinder, so the cylinder no longer had to be cooled and reheated every stroke; fuel consumption per unit of work fell several-fold compared with the Newcomen engine.

history.title: Carnot's Réflexions
history.detail: Sadi Carnot showed that the work obtainable from heat depends on the temperatures between which an engine operates, setting the upper bound that every thermal plant in this course is measured against.

history.title: Otto's four-stroke engine
history.detail: Nicolaus August Otto's compressing four-stroke gas engine, built at Deutz, established the cycle still used by spark-ignition engines.

history.title: Central power stations
history.detail: Thomas Edison's Pearl Street Station in New York began selling electricity from steam-driven dynamos in September 1882, the model for the utility power station.

history.title: Parsons's steam turbine
history.detail: Charles Parsons patented and built a multi-stage reaction steam turbine driving a dynamo; within a few decades turbines had replaced reciprocating engines in power stations.

history.title: The diesel engine is proven
history.detail: Rudolf Diesel's compression-ignition engine (German patent 67207, applied for in 1892) passed its acceptance test by Moritz Schröter in February 1897 with an overall efficiency of about 26 %, far above contemporary steam engines.

history.title: The Betz limit
history.detail: Albert Betz published the actuator-disc result that no wind turbine can extract more than 16/27 of the kinetic energy flux through its swept area; Lanchester (1915) and Zhukovsky (1920) reached the same limit independently.

history.title: First power-generating gas turbine
history.detail: Brown Boveri's 4 MW gas turbine at Neuchâtel, Switzerland, entered service with a generator-terminal efficiency of 17.4 %, measured in acceptance tests supervised by Aurel Stodola.

history.title: Nuclear power and the silicon solar cell
history.detail: The 5 MW Obninsk reactor in the USSR became the first nuclear plant to supply a power grid, and at Bell Laboratories Chapin, Fuller and Pearson demonstrated the first practical silicon photovoltaic cell.

history.title: Paris Agreement
history.detail: The parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change adopted the goal of holding warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels, which frames most current energy-system planning.

references.authors: Yunus A. Çengel, Michael A. Boles and Mehmet Kanoğlu
references.note: The prerequisite text; its steam, refrigerant and air tables and its chapters on vapour, gas and refrigeration cycles are the basis of the thermal chapters.

references.title: Combined-Cycle Gas & Steam Turbine Power Plants (3rd ed.)
references.authors: Rolf Kehlhofer, Frank Hannemann, Franz Stirnimann and Bert Rukes
references.note: Practical design of gas turbines, heat-recovery steam generators and combined-cycle and cogeneration plants.

references.title: Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals (2nd ed.)
references.note: The standard reference on engine thermodynamics, combustion, performance and emissions.

references.title: ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals
references.note: Psychrometrics, refrigerant properties and load-calculation methods used in air-conditioning practice.

references.title: Solar Engineering of Thermal Processes, Photovoltaics and Wind (5th ed.)
references.authors: John A. Duffie, William A. Beckman and Nathan Blair
references.note: Solar geometry, radiation data, collector analysis (Hottel–Whillier–Bliss) and system simulation.

references.title: Wind Energy Handbook (3rd ed.)
references.authors: Tony Burton, Nick Jenkins, Ervin Bossanyi, David Sharpe and Michael Graham
references.note: Actuator-disc and blade-element momentum theory, wind statistics, turbine loads and design.

references.title: Energy Storage: Fundamentals, Materials and Applications (2nd ed.)
references.note: Physical, thermal and electrochemical storage from first principles.
